utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott, do you have anything to address to this Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the witness, just so the record is clear, we compute the time used by the Prosecution yesterday, actual court time, not counting breaks, actual examination, at three hours, and of course our time has not yet started today. So we've not started yet today, you will note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. We should not argue it again. We spent so much time on that. We understand that this witness is a very important witness. It's worth spending much more time, you know, on this witness. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting for that long time. As you know, there were some housekeeping matters we have to deal with first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I can have the usher's assistance, I would like to address a couple of matters arising from yesterday which the Court had some questions about, and if we could distribute Exhibits 542.1 and 192.1, please, to the counsel, the courtroom, and the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are these in the binders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, these are the two documents the Chamber asked me -- the Chamber directed me to produce yesterday, and that's what I'm doing. And counsel's copies will -- please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, with respect to you, showing respect to you, and with respect to the Chamber's direction, we have provided to you this morning two documents that were referred to yesterday but which were not -- we were not able to put in front of you at that time. So I want you to be able to see those now. First, let me ask you to look at P542.1. This was the document that was questions about the mobilisation order, if I can call it that, on the 28th of July, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll let counsel ask -- direct ultimately any additional questions about that item to you. And I would also ask you to look -- or Chamber, for that matter. I'd also like you, Witness, to look at Exhibit 192.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be allowed to reply to this document, to respond, and not just to look at the document? He's looking at it for the first time, so may he be allowed to comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If he wishes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I have read the document. I have had time to do so. First of all, let me say that I did not write or sign this document. The signatory of this document -- the signature to this document is not mine. That's the first point. Secondly, this, viewed militarily, is an ordinary order on placing units on combat readiness. It is not an order for mobilisation. I do not know anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Well, again, my point at this moment is not to argue the document with you, simply that you have the chance to look at it. It is direct -- sir, you've said it's not your signature. It is prepared over the words, is it not, "Major General Slobodan Praljak"? And this was the time, as you've testified in these proceedings, when you were indeed the commander of the HVO Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just so there is no misunderstanding, the English translation does not correspond to the Croatian original. Had that been so, before this question that has just been asked by the Prosecutor, the word "za," meaning "for," would have been seen, apparent, and that word "for" - "za" - does not exist in the English version but it does in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't -- my question did not suggest for a moment that it was signed. I accepted the witness's testimony that it was not his signature and my pending question to him did not suggest otherwise. I simply said the order itself is typed for the signature of - and it has on it - and you can see it on the original B/C/S version as well - Major General Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question stands, sir. You were the commander of the HVO Main Staff on the 28th of July, 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us return to yesterday's day. This is what the Prosecutor said to the witness to trick him. "You wrote out an order to raise combat readiness for you to be able to do such and such in Stolac." That's what the Prosecutor said. Now, he has found the document, he has given it to the witness to have a look, and the witness says, "It is not my signature." Now, what are we going to do about what happened yesterday? Yesterday, the witness was exposed to cross-examination saying, "You expelled people from Stolac. You destroyed some mosques. And to bear that out, I have your order." Now we see the order, which has not been translated as it should have been, because in the Croatian language, the word "za" - z-a - exists meaning "for." So somebody else signed the order instead of the general, and this is a daily routine order that is issued for any type of combat readiness or raising the level. Now, what are we going to do with yesterday's question by the Prosecutor as it was asked, as it stood? That is precisely why we asked to have the documents shown, for the witness to be able to have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, when we weigh that evidence, we will take your objections into consideration and we will compare it with the transcript yesterday. There is no problem about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour, and that is why I asked for this, and during the private session, we said that the Prosecutor should show proof and evidence. Otherwise, he is trying to trip the witness up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We quite understand that. And, Witness, could you answer the question put forward by the Prosecutor just now? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Maybe, Mr. Scott, you could repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course. Mr. President, so that the Prosecution case is clear, this -- we don't submit that this changes anything that was put to the witness yesterday. It was put to the witness that as the commander, he presided over an action and that an order was issued, and of course the transcript will speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is: I'm not suggesting -- please listen to my question. I'm not suggesting that's your signature. You were the commander of the HVO Main Staff on the 28th of July, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, to your last question, that is to say whether on the 28th of July, 1993, I was commander of the Main Staff, my answer to that is yes, and I have been saying yes for two days now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That answers my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, please, you said that I commanded the operation, and I did not agree fully with that part of your observation, because I don't think I was at the -- at that time either in Capljina or Stolac, in that area, but that I was in Gornji Vakuf, Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look, please at Exhibit P192.1, you will see that, as I indicated to you yesterday, isn't it correct, sir - and can you confirm to us on the second page -- on the original, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On this original, you have my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the record will reflect that the factual assertions I made yesterday are reflected on this document, and I won't question it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in continuing on, can you please ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours, no, no. That's not true. That's not correct. Mr. Prosecutor, we are checking the transcript. The Prosecutor was not speaking about this letter but quite another letter. We are checking out the transcript. He was speaking about a letter that was sent to President Tudjman, and I asked him to show the letter, and he said that he would show it today, whereas he turns up with a letter now which speaks about a salary for Colonel Siljeg and now confirms that he has completed his task here. I really don't know what's going on. Do I really have to control who says what in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree completely. The record will speak for itself. This is the letter that I referred to and indicate that the transcript reflect that. I put the questions to this witness about whether he had signed a document concerning this matter, about the payment of this man, and whether he in fact was in the 115th HV Brigade. So I disagree with counsel. Obviously the transcript will make clear what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, let us not spend much time on this issue. We'll check the transcript during the breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours. Yes, there was a question about salaries, but it wasn't the letter we asked the representative of the Prosecution to provide, and he is obstructing matters and proceedings today. He is obstructing them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have to move, Witness. I think this issue is over for this moment, for this moment. We will look into the transcript, to see which letter it is. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to go back to this Mr. Zarko Tole momentarily because it wasn't entirely clear to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness would like to respond to the question asked about this document. He must clarify the document but nobody is giving him a chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Krsnik, this Trial Chamber has said we'll look into the transcript and to see which letter it is. That's a very clear message. We hope it could stop here and moving faster. Yes, Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning Mr. Zarko Tole, sir, can you indicate what was his position in the Bosnian Croat defence forces in 1992? What position or function did he serve during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Zarko Tole, in 1992, was in Bugojno, where he was taken prisoner by the Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Prior to the time that he was taken prisoner, sir - can you answer my question - what was his role or function or position at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know whether he was something the equivalent of a brigade commander or an operative zone commander or some such thing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention, then, to 1993, can you tell the Chamber what his function or role was in the Bosnian Croat armed forces in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in 1993, as commander of the Croatian Defence Council, Mr. Zarko Tole was the head of -- chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, HVO. The structure that we had at the time, of course, doesn't correspond -- wouldn't correspond to normal-day situations in regular armies, because in a regular, normal army, the chief of the Main Staff is the person who is in charge, whereas we, faced with a highly complicated situation on the front, on the battleground, faced with a large Muslim offensive in 1993, we had both a commander, an HVO commander, and a deputy commander of the Main Staff as well, and the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Who was --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is highly unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may be. So Mr. Tole in 1993, you've said, was the chief of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so. It is correct that he was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Petkovic's position in 1993? What was Mr. Petkovic in 1993, if he was not chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I provided an exhaustive answer. He was deputy commander of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council, Mr. Petkovic that is. I was the commander of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council and Zarko Tole was the head or chief of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council, and this is a very unusual structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... are you indicating that Mr. Tole was your deputy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I was asked to do when I cross-examined, could the Prosecutor please explain the relevance of these questions and why are these questions asked now when we have other facts for which this witness was called? Why are these questions relevant and important for the Prosecutor? Unless he's conducting some private investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, you have to tell us the relevance of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. President, the Defence presented us this chart, and we have been asking and trying to understand since yesterday the command structure that this witness -- where he fit into it. And we've gotten a number, a range of answers from, "No function, no position, I just went down there, I just showed up in Bosnia and did things," and we are continuing to try to understand where this witness fit in the command structure and his relationship with other senior commanders. We do not have that -- in our respectful submission, Mr. President, we have not yet been given that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you are challenging the credibility of this witness, you may continue. But don't move too far away from the subject matter of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, are you telling us, sir - I'm trying to understand -- sir, let me finish my question, if I could, please. Are you indicating that Mr. Tole was your deputy at the time you became the chief of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I believe that my answers are precise and sincere. I was the commander of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council at the time indicated here. I was the one. Mr. Milivoj Petkovic was my deputy. And Mr. Zarko Tole was the third-ranking man in the structure as the head, as the head of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council. I never evaded giving you a precise answer. And I'm sorry if it is not up to your expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before you became chief of the Main Staff in approximately mid-July, 1993, then, do I understand you correctly to be saying that prior to that time, Mr. Petkovic was the chief officer, military officer, in command of the HVO? Let's say from January -- for these purposes, let's say from January 1 of 1993, until you took that position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered that four times. The same question is being asked for the fourth time. I don't know if we are sitting in two different courtrooms, and I apologise, or is it perhaps that the translation is such that I do not know what this is all about? I am sorry, I'm saying that this was asked and answered repeatedly. That is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, you may explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The witness asked -- answered the question just now as of the time in mid-July, 1993, that he became the chief of the HVO. He told us yesterday, I believe - I'm trying to clarify in light of his answer just now - who was the chief commander, if you will, what position - we seem to get into arguments about words - who was the senior HVO officer prior to his time. Now, I think he said it was Mr. Petkovic, and I don't understand why that's so confusing, except I'm just trying to confirm that that in fact is his answer because he gave us the answer only as of the time he assumed his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is: Before you took on the position of chief of the HVO, is it correct, then, that from January 1st, 1993, until you took that position, we understand correctly then that Mr. Petkovic was the senior officer in command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe even before that, that is even before the 1st of January, 1993, from April, 1992, Mr. Petkovic was the head of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council, from April, 1992, and that is another thing that I have repeated several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Tole - and this is, I hope, the last question concerning this - Mr. Tole then, before the time that you became chief of the Main Staff in mid-July, was Mr. Tole also number 2 or the deputy to Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Mr. Tole was in the Serb -- in a Serb camp for a long time, and how a long time was spent trying to get Mr. Tole back, I do not know exactly when he came and what duty he took up in the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council. But I know exactly what he was when I arrived there in July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher's assistance to give the witness Exhibit D1/82 which is the chart, Your Honours, that was tendered by the Defence? And I have prepared an English -- had prepared an English translation, which may assist. You can use my -- well, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at the B/C/S, the original coloured version, picking up on the questions that were asked yesterday -- some of the questions that were asked yesterday, as of the time that you became the chief of the HVO Main Staff, are you in the top -- or do you place yourself then in that top, red box, which in English would be something interpreted as supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could you put the chart on the ELMO, please? The English one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you have to be more precise. When you ask Mr. Praljak to look at the map and to say what this position was, could you specify the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think I did, Your Honour, but probably not well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you took your position, sir, in mid-July, 1993 - I'm directing your attention to that point in time - did your position then -- is it reflected in the top, red box in the coloured version of the document? If not, say so. But tell us where you fit on this chart as of mid-July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are talking about mid-July, and I arrived later, and there is the exact date, and you are trying to shift my arrival forward, and my answer to your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the date that you assumed that position -- I don't want to argue you about that. On the date you took that position, where were you on this chart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you do not want to argue about this, then start mentioning the date "as of the date when you arrived," so as not to try to intimate some other date. And secondly, I was the commander of this box here. I was at the top of this box.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which box again? Would you take a marker, please, sir? I'm going to ask you -- and I'll have this marked as a new exhibit once the witness has made his markings -- if you can provide a marking on where you say you fit on this chart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the title says that this is the diagram of the HVO structure from 1993, and we have the witness's precise answer when that was, I think it would be fair to him to also put the date next to this box, the date when he assumed the duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if possible.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Thank you. And that's exactly why I'm asking you to look at this chart, to avoid confusion, because in the box it says "Supreme Commander." That may have been misinterpreted to be Chief Commander, or whatever you -- Chief of the Main Staff. So when in this chart it says "Supreme Commander," as of the date you've now written, the 27th of July, 1993, who was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you write that on the chart, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as of July 27, 1993, who was the - whatever term you want - minister or secretary of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please write that on the chart.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, please, looking at this chart, can you tell us where the Convicts' Battalion fits on this chart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you mark that, please. Why don't you put K -- well, you can put whatever you like. I suggest you might put "KB."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, where Mladen Naletilic would appear on this chart? In the structure, where would you put him on this chart?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was not the commander of the Convicts' Battalion, and I do not really know where to fit him in this chart, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us -- are you familiar with groups that were called anti-terrorist groups, or ATGs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, groups of that kind, those autonomous units, the structure of that army, when a street would rally, or a village, or a part of a town, and it was like that, that at some points in time, the HVO had several hundred units fluctuating in this whole structure as voluntary, relatively poorly organised military structure. I keep repeating that. This was the zero option of the armed people, and in spite of my best wishes to help you and this Honourable Court, I cannot answer and threaten the truth by giving some other answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me ask you some additional specific questions, then. You were, as of the 27th of July, 1993, the chief of this organisation, or a large measure of it. Were the ATGs part of the units for special assignments and professional units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were units which could be called up to take part in an action. They did not stay on the positions, and a large number of those guys wanted to have units of their own, a unit gathered around them, because that made them feel special.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you saying these were private armies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, they were not private armies. But between what we call a private army and what we may term as a good and fully structured army, there is a very broad range, a very broad span of something in between. And that also varied from one month to the other in that war, both with regard to the quality of the structuring and the dispersion of the army, depending on the quality and the progress of political negotiations and the situation on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you put them in the headquarters' unit's box, then, the next box down, the darker blue box in the coloured version. So do the ATGs fit in that box?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also those attached to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, they were in the HQ unit's box?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The ATGs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not all of them. We had such units. I had two such units: Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I thought - and correct me if I'm wrong - my understanding had been that they would - of course, it doesn't matter - but those were part -- those were professional units in the top box: Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those attached to the HQ are the two down there. But I repeat once again: I cannot -- there did not exist such an organisation, such type of organisation that would enable me to answer this with yes or no, and thus fully reflect the truth that I wish to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And were the ATGs, then -- did they fit under the structure of the various operative zones, then? Did they fit in one of the boxes on the bottom part of the chart? Let's direct our attention, for these purposes, to the Operative Zone Mostar. Did the ATGs that operated in the Mostar Operative Zone, were they in that box?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an ATG went to the front line, then whilst at the front line, it would be subordinated to the commander of that front. But when it would no longer be used for combat purposes at a particular front line, we did not have barracks, any barracks, so we didn't know where this group went. And that is why I'm saying that this was armed people who, at certain points in time, after a certain rest, because nobody was on the front line all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who would contact these groups, as you say, and then subordinate them to a particular operation or unit for combat purposes? Someone had to contact them and say, "Please report to this location for duty." Who did that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the operative zone did that, or somebody from the Main Staff, or somebody on his own, privately. There was -- commands were issued, and I do not try to shunt the responsibility for commanding, insofar as it is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say someone --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But never --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- how would someone privately call up one of the ATGs to combat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simple: "I'm faced with a difficult situation. We lose this position. We need help."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're telling us, sir, to use a specific example for this case, and I'm just simply -- one that people will recognise: The Benko Penavic -- I won't use Vinko Skrobo, some distance from one of the accused. But let's take the Benko Penavic ATG. Are you saying that any commander anywhere in Herceg-Bosna, if they felt the need, could contact the head of the Benko Penavic and say, "Hey, come over and help me"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those who knew them, you know, because this is a small area and many people are related, so they all knew one another. Troops knew one another. I don't know if somebody from Central Bosnia could send such an invitation, could issue such a call, but down there, yes, of course, and also it could be the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, all right, sir. Just to finish on the ATGs, and I'm just trying to understand, then, to conclude this. You decline to put the ATGs in any box, in any particular box on this chart; is that what you're telling the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did, in a fluctuating structure, in this box here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're talking about the bigger -- counsel -- my colleague has asked me to be clear. Are you talking about the light-blue box, the top light-blue box on the right side of the coloured chart? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Why don't you put to that -- would you please mark that "ATGs," however you want to qualify it, sir. "Sometimes"? I don't want to be accused of characterising your evidence, so -- "ATG on some occasions," whatever you like to say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, trying to finish up on this chart, let me ask you this: The way the chart has been prepared -- let me ask you, sir: Did you assist in preparing this chart or was this something that was just provided to you at some point?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not assist in preparing this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you first see it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was shown to me by the counsel when I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps you can assist us, then. There are, from the Supreme Commander box, the top box, the Defence Department box, and the Main Staff box, there are lines coming out to the right side, and then there's a line that goes to that special assignments, special purpose units box to the right. Now, is this to indicate, sir, if you know, did any of those groups - the Supreme Commander, the Defence Department, or the Main Staff - each equally command or call upon the units in that box?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, because I want to be as close to the truth as possible, when we talked about nationalism, what we tried to say when we were talking about nationalism, and that is, there is serious trouble with words, with their contents, to command everybody, all, because these terms, when uttered like this, then they mean organisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you just so I can assist you, please, so we can go forward. Strike the word "command." Tell the Chamber, please: The lines that come out from the right side of those boxes and go to the special purposes and professional units box - I won't characterise them in any way - you tell us: What do those lines indicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without denying the chain of command and the structure of the army, there was, between people who performed various duties in all these boxes, a much closer connection, and this is service of a cause. And this is a correct chart, a correct representation, and it means that we could ask or issue an order, invite, request, the Supreme Commander, the Defence Department, the Main Staff. The situation was so difficult, so tense, that I do not recall, Mr. Prosecutor, that during my stay there in 1993 I spent two nights in one and the same bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without avoiding --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I guess you've answered the question the best you can. Let me give you a specific example, if it assists. You testified a few moments ago that Bruno Stojic was the head of the Defence Department. Now, does this chart indicate -- could he call up and issue commands to a professional unit without going to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he could have done it, but it was usually done by agreement. He could not command that unit once it had arrived at the front line - defence line, excuse me - with somebody because of poor communications or because I was too far away, because Mr. Petkovic was somewhere far away, that Mr. Tole was somewhere on the ground, and the situation made it imperative. Then it would -- then one could go through Mr. Stojic to ask him to send a unit. But once that unit arrived at the front, it would become a part of the structure commanded by somebody from the Operative Zone or that front line to which they had come, more narrowly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I ask just one final question on this, I hope, and then we'll move --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just to finish on that, sir. You said someone -- to use the example we're using, Mr. Stojic could call up and send the unit, but once the unit was on the ground, so to speak, it would be subordinate to some other commander. Let me just give you the opposite of that however. It is also that someone -- and again, we're simply using Mr. Stojic's one example. Could Mr. Stojic withdraw that unit, unsubordinate, if you will, or withdraw a unit from its location?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it withdrew from a site when its term expired, when its tour of duty expired and when they were to have a rest. I don't remember him doing it, and it depended on the front line situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you finish this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On this chart, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the witness, I think there is some clarification to make. During the break, we checked the transcript. The first one is that there was a suggestion of the Defence that the Prosecution brought the wrong letter. In the transcript, page 9525, line 20 to 25 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecution referred to a letter to Mr. Ivan Cermak, dated November 12. On page 9526, line 10 to 13, the Defence asked the Prosecutor to bring this letter. On page 9526, line 20 to 22, the Presiding Judge ordered the Prosecution to bring the letter. The result is the exhibit brought today is the letter requested by the Defence. The second issue is there was a claim of the Defence that they requested to see the letter of Mr. Praljak to Mr. Tudjman. On page 9534, line 3 to 6 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecution asked the witness if he sent a resignation letter to Mr. Tudjman and the witness confirmed it. So we believe there was no argument about the existence or the contents of this letter. And it's also agreed by the Defence side. Having said that, Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have the usher's assistance, please, in putting Exhibit 587.2, the English version, on the ELMO, please, and the B/C/S version to the witness? I'm sorry it should be in that separate package. Excuse me, Your Honour, this is the separate package that I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the last page of the original B/C/S version, can you please confirm that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature is on the last page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to the first paragraph on the first page, right under, "I hereby order," and number 1, you say, "The operative zone," and I believe - and please correct me, sir, if I'm wrong - I think that's the operative zone for Southeastern Herzegovina, and then you give a list of units, and if you go through the paragraph, please, a few lines down, it includes the Mrmak units and the Benko Penavic ATG. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Will you tell us, then, are you saying that the result of this order was that those two ATGs were operating under the operative zone commander for the Southeast Herzegovina operative zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those units, when they were on the line, they were operating under the commander of the operative zone of Southeast Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, now, it may be helpful if we have the usher's -- the witness still has available to him the organisational chart, D1/82. Better be clear here, sir, for some different terminology has been used on the chart. Am I correct to suggest that when the charts use the term "OZ Mostar," could that also be the same, for these purposes, as saying -- could have been also described as the operative zone, Southeast Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Both terms were used: Operative Zone Mostar and Operative Zone South-east Herzegovina. It was the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, why don't we -- it could come up, Mr. President, in the future, so if assists the Chamber, let's just finish that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next one, OZ Tomislav, that would correspond to the North-west Herzegovina Operative Zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is also referred to with two terms: the Operative Zone Tomislav and the Operative Zone of the North-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. North-east or north-west?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: North-west. I'm sorry. I meant north-west. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the OZ Vitez was also known as the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was also known as the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the fourth box, the last box to the right on the chart, what would be the other name or the other reference for that Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operative Zone of Bosanski Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that the area that was up on the border in North-east Bosnia, on the border of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: North, towards the Croatian border. Orasje, Derventa, Slavonski Brod, that belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, if we take, then, your order of the 1st of September 1993, Exhibit 587.2, and the organisational chart together, what your order says -- am I correct, then, to understand that by your order of the 1st of September, the ATG Mrmak and the ATG Benko Penavic were placed under the command in that far box to the bottom left, the OZ Mostar? That's where we would put them on the chart at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operative Zone Mostar, and within the Mostar Operative Zone, the town of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So then, according to your chart, then, to use this chart and your order together, then, as of that date, as of the 1st of September, the ATG Mrmak ultimately under your chain of command, wasn't it, since you are the Glavni Stozer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During, that is to say, while those units were up at the front line, the chain of command went up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Therefore, sir, you would be responsible for the behaviour of those units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to keep objecting, Your Honour. You see, I haven't been objecting. I think that the witness has come here to explain everything and to tell the truth. But I have an ongoing objection to make, and it is the following: This Trial Chamber should caution the witness that if the Prosecutor asks questions in the manner he is doing, the witness need not answer. I think that the Trial Chamber could warn the witness of that, because possibly, possibly, more time would be required and explanations required, if he were to put himself in the position of being persecuted. So my objection, in short, is that the Trial Chamber should step in and should warn the witness about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we believe that before the witness came here, it's your responsibility to warn your witness about incriminating himself. I understand that the witness is asking a question, that is, in what sense? Mr. Scott, you may explain to this witness what's your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the military chain of command, does not the head of the Operative Zone Mostar, or South-east Herzegovina, whichever phrase we want to use, then was reporting for these purposes, was under your command, and reported to you and took orders from you under the military chain of command, as depicted on D1/82; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this is a very sensitive issue and question, I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to give a broader answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Since this issue is very important, you may have more explanations on this issue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer as to whether the chain of command goes up to me, the answer to that is yes. The chain of command does reach me, as the main commander of the Croatian Defence Council. But the chain of command is not a chain of responsibility vis-a-vis possible incriminations which an individual, within the frameworks of an army that I command, or a unit which is within the army that I command, that I should be held responsible for their acts. Let me quote an example. The great massacre in Vietnam, in My Lai, for instance, when the American General learnt about what actually happened two years later, and he was not held responsible for the acts committed, although he was the commander of that particular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this. If one of the -- if your order of the 1st of September had not been carried out, if one of these units had refused the assignment reflected on your order, you would have been in a position to discipline or punish or refer for court martial the refusing officer, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So your order is that -- your September 1st order was meaningless and there was no sanction for violating your order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order wasn't meaningless because it was based upon a -- far more on the voluntary character and the desire to defend a certain territory than on military discipline and organisation, as is recognised in the armies whose contents of the concept of army and army organisation you wish to transplant to the Croatian Defence Council and have it apply there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Look at the entire order, please, and I want you to point out to the Judges - not for my benefit - I want you to point out to the Judges where in that order it says, "This is my -- these are the orders or my assignments, if you feel like it. You can do this if you want but if you don't want, doesn't matter." Show us that language, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do you think I ought to write that down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't say write it down. I said, please in your order, please find the language which says, "Compliance with this order is at -- if you want to. If you don't want to, okay."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered your question very exactly, Mr. Prosecutor. The force of this order was far more reliant upon the consciousness and awareness of the individuals who made up these units, rather than the possibility of a military organisation, which I stood at the head, to sanction and punish the individuals if they did not comply. Now, for -- in tens of -- there were many occasions where units left their positions of their own volition. Regardless of what I would write, the requests I would make for measures to punish them, there was no organisational form or power, organisational power and authority, to implement that in full, to put it into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Well, if we have time, we will maybe come back to that issue, if we can. Sir, is it correct that during the time that you were operating in Bosnia, starting at least in November, 1992, that you used the code name Brada, B-r-a-d-a?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, would you always refer to it as Bosnia-Herzegovina, please? Because the state of Bosnia does not exist. The state that does exist is called Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was called by different names, and I think that they sometimes referred to me as Brada too, although I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, who gave you that -- who gave you the code name Brada?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do you really think I can answer that question who called me Brada first? It's not a code name. It's a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Well can I ask you to look --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher put on the ELMO the English version of 463.1 and show the witness the B/C/S version, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is this an order issued in a field -- in a packet of communication?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this an order issued by Paket communication to Bruno Stojic on the 17th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed all my orders, and to be frank, I would never write anything like this, "Urgent, urgently answer." It's not my style. And quite certainly I did not write this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you had assistants, deputies, aides de camp, didn't you? We are not -- I don't think anyone is suggesting that you necessarily wrote and sent every order yourself, but this is an order you sent; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of order -- actually, it's not an order. It's a questionnaire -- a question. It is not an order. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could please show the witness 463.2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I don't think the witness answered the previous question. Did he sign that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you'll look at the -- I agree with the Chamber that he didn't, but if you look at the original version of the order -- and of course, you don't -- Mr. Usher, could you put the B/C/S version of that last exhibit on the ELMO, please? Your Honour, this is what this looks like, and I submit to you - and I would hope at this point there might not be a dispute about this - this is an electronic field communication, a fax or a Paket -- what's sometimes called a Paket communication, and I'm going to suggest that, in very rough and simplistic terms, perhaps something what we might call an e-mail today. Of course, there is no handwritten signature on an e-mail. It's an electronic communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question -- doesn't it indicate, sir, on that -- isn't that the format that you're familiar with which indicates that the communication was sent, the date of the communication, when it was sent out? Don't you see that on there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again, there are questions, not answers. The question would be: Was he aware of, did he sign, does he know how this was sent? Now we heard testimony in fact from the Prosecutor, through his questions. This is something that he should be asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Prosecution is asking the witness the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let the witness answer, then. The witness has not answered those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm only too happy -- this is the question that was first put to the witness about five or ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this an order or communication that was sent under your authority, sir, on the 17th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an order. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you send it, sir? Was it sent on your authorisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is not my style, and it was not sent on my authorisation, and I don't remember having been up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Will you please look at 463.2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't this, in fact, a response to your communication received from -- coming back from Colonel Akrap?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the response to the person who sent that question, and if I tell you that I did not, then why are you telling me that this is the answer to my question, the question that I did not send out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The person addressed here, sir, Breda, that was you, wasn't it? Brada, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not me. Brada mentioned here, that is not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Well do you know who that Brada is, then? If it's your position it is somebody else, then please tell us who.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there were so many nicknames, Stari, Brada, Sesir, Dugi. Do you know that I can tell you how many Bradas there were?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me help you, sir. How many Bradas do you know that could issue a communication directly to the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I do not know a single Brada who could do that, and I don't think I would have to know that, nor is it up to me to know who wrote this, nor is this something that could have anything to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You're keeping standing, interrupting the testimony of your witness. That's not fair. What we want to hear is what the witness is going to tell us, no matter you agree with it or not. Unless there is a very substantial issue, very important issues, then you may interrupt, but judging from the previous practices, we don't believe it's useful for to you be standing up from time to time. Yes, you may have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is why I stood up. It is not really my fault that I have to stand up so often, because I do not see this document say Bruno Stojic anywhere, and I do not know how can the Prosecutor claim that this is -- that this was sent to Bruno Stojic? This document shows clearly who it was sent to and who signed it, and I simply want to say that the cross-examination needs to be correct, and this is not what it says here. It was not sent to the ministry. It says to the operative zone of Northwest Herzegovina. Where is Bruno Stojic here? The witness perhaps is not up to the tricks of cross-examination, and I simply say that we need to ensure fair treatment, but that is all and I won't be standing up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, your intervention is a little bit off the track. From the transcript, I thought that the witness gave a good answer to the question, but don't mislead us to somewhere else. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you may wish to look back at the prior exhibit, 463.1, and that communication, which is certainly at the very least over your name, Major General Praljak, is going to Bruno Stojic in person. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that because it says so here in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, what is your testimony as to the role, then, position of Mladen Naletilic in the Bosnian Croat armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I think I've answered that question several times already, I will do so again. In a nutshell, I left Siroki Brijeg when I was 15 and I met Mr. Naletilic when I was close to 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is not responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we have heard that experience with Mr. Naletilic, but here the question asked by the Prosecution is that: "What is your testimony as to the role, then, the position of Mladen Naletilic in the Bosnian Croat armed forces?" It's a very simple question. Concentrate on this question, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I commanded the Croat Defence Council in 1993, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was not ever under my command. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Whose command was he under?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look, please -- if the usher can show you Exhibit P111.1. Thank you. Can you provide any assistance to the Chamber, please, on why it would be that Tuta, in combination with Bruno Stojic, would be signing a document giving movement, essentially a movement permit, permission for free movement, to a member of the Convicts' Battalion named Goran Andric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you will have to ask Mr. Bruno Stojic, the minister or the head of the Ministry of Defence of the Croat Defence Council at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what was Mr. Naletilic's relationship to the Convicts' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher please show you P172.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you agree, sir, that Mr. Naletilic was a member or employee of the HVO Defence Department, or the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, on the 10th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither agree nor disagree. I was the commander of the Main Staff, and the Defence Department was not under me; it was above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask the interpreters for some assistance, please. In the sentence that says confirming that Mr. Naletilic - I'm sorry - Mladen Naletilic is an employee of the Defence Department, can that also be interpreted to say "is a member of the Defence Department"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would have to see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Of course. Thank you. Can I ask the usher to please show you Exhibit 341. Mr. President, just to assist the Registry, I think the vast majority of the documents that will be used will be in that bundle, so you shouldn't -- they shouldn't have to be looking for documents. They should be in the bundle that's been given to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall, on about the 25th of April, 1993, issuing a communication, being involved in a communication to the effect: For Tuta. Brada requests urgent meeting in Siroki Brijeg. Say when reply urgently. Bruno approves Dragan staying with Siljeg. Do you remember sending that communication or having it sent for you -- or to - excuse me - to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall the message. I fail to see its sense, what it means. I do not know who Jezicic [phoen] is. And if I wanted to communicate with Mr. Mladen Naletilic, then I could do it without sending such messages --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How would you do it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if I ever thought that necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How would you communicate with Tuta, then, if you didn't have to resort to this manner?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By telephone. We had telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall why it was urgent for you to meet with Mr. Tuta in Siroki Brijeg on the 25th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I deny in toto the sense of this document and say that it had nothing to do with me, then your question why was this meeting to be held is a very crude insinuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Remind the Chamber, please. It may have come up before. Please assist us. Who is Zeljko Akrap?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Akrap was an officer in the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council at the time when I was the commander of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Doesn't it say "Main Staff Duty Officer"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer is like a medical nurse. What it means is simply that you don't sleep the night, and it doesn't mean that he wasn't an officer in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... another one of these officers who came -- who was an HVO officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that he was not an -- that he was an officer. Excuse me. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall that -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stringer informs me that the last question and answer wasn't in the transcript. The question to the witness was:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that Mr. Akrap was another one of these HV officers assisting the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall that the 25th of April, 1993 was during the HVO action at Sovici Doljani?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was not in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore whatever I say would be only based on hearsay, based on stories, rather than as the one who was there and who eyewitnessed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how much of the time were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the spring of 1993, then? Please tell us. Were you there one day and three months or were you there every day except one day and three months?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I believe I answered -- I gave a rather exhaustive answer to that question, I would need to have an IBM computer in place of my brain to be able to answer, after ten years, questions which are phrased in this manner in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Praljak, you were able to answer very detailed questions on direct examination, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the brain has a selective memory. Some things, some events, some dates stick, are imprinted on one's memory, and I'm confident about them, and that is how I presented them and how I answered during the direct examination and whenever you ask me questions related to them. Of course, if I had time, and if those questions were submitted to me in writing, and if the Honourable Court would care to hear about this, would be interested in hearing about this, then I could provide more precise answers, either in writing or by coming again to this courtroom. But do not expect from me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, when Mr. Scott, the Chief Prosecutor in this action, asked you whether the dates, the operative dates, the 25th of April, was during the HVO action at Sovici and Doljani, you answered very promptly and immediately that, "At that time I was not in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and you explained that your evidence would therefore not be of great assistance to the Court. Now you're saying you'd need an IBM computer to recall where you were. Perhaps you'd tell the Court, and we would be greatly assisted if you could say why you were so positive that on the 25th of April, 1993, you were not in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do that, Your Honour, because I heard about those actions, I listened about them, and I know because of that. I'm quite sure that I was not there, because some actions -- because important actions are -- one remembers important actions if one was there or was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were back -- weren't you back, then, in Bosnia-Herzegovina around that time when you attended, with Mr. Tuta, Naletilic - excuse me - at the funeral of Mr. Cikota? And I can show you a photograph in a moment if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher assist me by showing the witness Exhibit P36. Can you put that on the ELMO, please. Can you lower that down a bit so we can get the -- okay. Either way. Either the technical booth or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's you standing on the far left side of that photograph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who is the person with the dark -- not the next person to your immediate -- your immediate in-the-picture left, the balding man, but in the middle of the picture approximately, in the camouflage uniform with glasses, who is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andabak, Mr. Andabak, Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to Mr. Andabak's immediate left in the photograph, who is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You did attend Cikota's funeral, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I attended Mr. Cikota's funeral, Mr. Mario Hrkac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in fact, sir, you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina toward the end of April, 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the day when Mr. Mario Hrkac, nicknamed Cikota, was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I have the usher's assistance please in going to Exhibit P399.2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You might be interested to hear, Mr. Praljak, that the Defence counsel for the other accused in this case, Mr. Martinovic, suggested that you were a constitutional lawyer from the court, and you'll be happy to hear that the person who was identifying you was convinced that it was you, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for always raising the right question, namely this is the gentleman who Mr. -- the Prosecutor skipped, and I see that it was deliberate. This is the gentleman who is standing next to Mr. Praljak, between Mr. Praljak and Mr. Andabak. That is the gentleman. Yes, yes, that's right, that is the gentleman I identified in the courtroom, and I showed his photograph and I asked Mr. Munje Printe [phoen] whether this was the gentleman that he had communicated with, and he said yes. And I said this was Mr. Vukojevic, a judge of the Constitutional Court, who is still on this photograph, and you can ask the witness whether I am right, and the Prosecutor forgot to ask who was the gentleman who was standing next to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We understood -- and certainly when I had the photograph, I thought it was Mr. Par who said that the person who was identified as General Praljak was actually a judge from the Constitutional Court, but if I'm wrong, I stand corrected. That's certainly the impression I had. But we won't debate about it. It's not important. There really is no reason to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it would be very important for the Court to show this man and to check this, because I remember every single sentence that I said on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You can do that on re-examination. It's not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to confirm that, Your Honour, it's not in dispute at this time. I could ask any number of questions about that photograph. I tried to ask the ones that were most pertinent to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if the usher could please assist you by showing you P399.2, again, sir, can you please assist the Chamber in any information that you can provide as to why it would be that on the 17th of May, 1993, Tuta would be co-signing an order with the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic, for the -- concerning the needs of 200 kilograms of -- and there is two documents here, and you'll see them and they have been put as one exhibit. You can certainly look at both of them. When you look at them together, 200 kilograms of some TNT shapes? Can you shed some light, please, on why it would be that Mr. Tuta would be issuing such an order, along with the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. Prosecutor, that I have absolutely no information about this, no knowledge. I know absolutely nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If the usher could please show you 564.1? When you look at the second page of the B/C/S original, sir, can you confirm to us that this is an order issued by you, or on your authority, whether it bears your signature or not, on the 12th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature. And I -- may I be given some time to read this, to see if I could write anything like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I commanded. I did not sign this and this is not my signature. Except -- with the exception of item 2 of this order, where RTP - and I have no idea what that is - then an air force group, of which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I've never heard, aircraft group, and Tuta ATG, which never existed, to my knowledge, as such, and I never commanded over anything of that kind. The rest basically is something that I could have signed but I did not. I did not write this and it is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand you to say correctly that everything in the document seems to be correct to you and you could have signed except for the very few items you specifically disagree with, one of them, of course, being the Tuta ATG reference?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reading it as I did now, at a glance, I do not know what could be in dispute here, but I repeat, RTP, aircraft group, Tuta ATG, DTC, all these things, I do not know what units are those and I never issued any orders to them. They were never under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps you can assist us in this way: You were the commander of the General Staff of the HVO on the 12th of August, 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it your -- perhaps we can just -- it may assist the Chamber -- is it going to be -- is it your position -- is it going to be your position that any order, any document, over your name but not bearing your personal signature is an invalid document? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The Commander of the Main Staff of the HVO signs his documents. The Deputy Commander of the Main Staff signs his orders in his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling us --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Main Staff signs his orders in his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're telling us -- excuse me, sir. You've given an answer. Let me follow up. You're telling us that as a senior officer, as with any -- many -- if it's in the military or not, senior executives, no one ever signed documents for you? You didn't have a deputy, a secretary, an aide de camp? Nobody ever signed a document for you, for -- on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army at war, that is not a rule, sir. Everybody is supposed to sign his own document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher please take the witness to Exhibit 662.01?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is your signature on that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Prosecutor. That is indeed my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in this document, sir, you are indicating -- you are listing a number of people who would be attending officer training at the HVU, that is the Croatian Military Academy, on the 2nd of November, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the people according to the units was done by the commanders of those units for a certain feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Perhaps you can answer my question. This was a communication, an order, as titled here, "Order," concerning the sending of officers for training at the Croatian Military Academy; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was a Croatian Military Academy in the Republic of Croatia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That academy was in the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to look at the first page after the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. President, in the English version, it's not translated because essentially it's just a list of names, so there is no English parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But if you look on the first list of names, sir, do you see two entries for someone going to this training from the Kaznjenicka Bojna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the Convicts Battalion, Mr. Prosecutor. That's where he's coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All these units were part of the HVO, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One does not necessarily follow from the other, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, is it your position, then, that the Kaznjenicka Bojna reflected on this document, that that unit was not part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From that time -- and we were talking about the place in the organisational chain where the Convicts Battalion was located, so I'm just sticking by the statements I made earlier, that the Convicts Battalion, during my time of command, was not under my command, unless it came up to the front line, when it entered the chain of command, and then, according to that chain of command, for that period of time, I happened to be at the top of the chain of command. Then that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, that wasn't exactly my question, whether you were in command. My question was: Is it your position that the Convicts Battalion was part of the HVO? Yes or no?
