utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the HVO is a broader concept than the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could assist us with the chart. I don't know if the witness still has the organisational chart or not, the one that he marked on. Perhaps that could be put on the ELMO, please, so that both the witness and everyone else can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated earlier today that the KB was in that first large box to the right. Are you telling the Chamber that that box is not part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that the HVO was a much broader concept than the army itself, than just the army. That does not mean that I'm saying something differently to what I said before, that this does not belong to the army, but this is just the military army part of the HVO, which had its government, its ministers, its jurisprudence, and jurisdiction, and all the other features, and that it was investing great efforts during these times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for translation. I'm sorry. Was the Convicts Battalion, on the 27th of July, 1993, and again when you issued this order on the 29th of October, 1993, was the Convicts Battalion part of the military HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, right where I'm indicating now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the usher please show you 662.02?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you sign that order on the 30th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, looking at the first page, reference number 3, "The Convicts Battalion and the Ludvig Pavlovic and the Grdani units are to be put on alert to be used as reserve units at the request of the HVO Main Staff." Sir, is it correct -- do I understand correctly that you are issuing an order here on the field disposition of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I did issue an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking to the second page -- it's the second page in the English version. It's the -- the B/C/S version is only one page. But to -- the information to the left of your signature, where it says -- one of the persons under the "delivered to," it says, "Convicts Battalion." Can you assist the Chamber, how would an order like that be communicated, and indeed, delivered, to the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These orders were sent by Paket link, by telephone, and conveyed orally. For example, as far as the Grdani unit is concerned, on many occasions they went in the field on the basis of a request rather than an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, my question to you was: How would this order be distributed to the Convicts' Battalion, please? Did someone drive it to Siroki Brijeg? Did someone from Siroki Brijeg come get it? Was it sent in the mail? Did the Convicts' Battalion get such orders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what way this particular one reached them, but they could have been sent by fax, by telephone, and orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Since it comes up from time to time, and you may have hesitated a moment ago about some question of it: Can you tell the Chamber, what was a Paket communication?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Paket communication is a type of electronic communication of data with encrypted -- a certain amount of encryption, encrypted protection. It is similar to a fax, but it is protected by code. But this isn't a very secure method, at least not in the conditions and circumstances in which we were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 5 on your order, I just want to ask you this. It says: "Submit a written report to me on the implementation of this order by 1000 hours on 31 of October, 1993." Now, is this another one of those orders which it's not really an order, so if someone had not given you the report by the 31st of October, it didn't really matter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, sir, is important, but if somebody did not submit a report, then I did not have at my disposal any means with which to punish or in any other way implement military will, for the simple reason that, as I said, it was far more an army based on voluntariness than organisation. But we did try to introduce the relationship of subordinate -- the subordinate relationship, and so the orders should have been the kind of orders that an army issues. But I assure you, Mr. Prosecutor, if I may be allowed to continue, that never and in no place would you find that this report on the situation came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're telling this Chamber that the HVO, and in particular, at the point of its evolution by the summer and fall of 1993, had no form of military discipline? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I said was that discipline was far more based on the sentiments and feeling of belonging, of being conscious of belonging to units which, in very strong onslaughts from the Muslim side, had to defend themselves, rather than being a form of discipline of the kind that armies have when we say, say, the American army, the French army, or the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to put it --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to finish, to complete my answer, please. If, Mr. Prosecutor, you wish us to establish what we mean by the word "army," the term "army," and when you say "army," you keep wanting us to bear in mind the American army and the French army, then unfortunately I have to tell you that we're not going to arrive at the truth speaking in that way, because these are tremendous efforts to have voluntary, organised groups of citizens form part of an organised system in times that were extremely difficult, and it was with enormous energy that we undertook to do that task. But to establish military organisation, even when a state is in existence, you need at least ten years for the task, and you'll find that in all textbooks that have been written on military matters. You'll be able to read about that there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can take a break there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Bring the witness in, please, Mr. Usher. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I don't think we will have time to cover this in any length at all in your testimony here on this occasion, but I want to put to you, sir, that there is extensive evidence that there was indeed a military discipline, military justice system, in place, that HVO soldiers were disciplined for any number of things, being absent without leave, not having -- having their weapons not clean. There was a military discipline system, wasn't there, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For certain soldiers, in certain units which were better, we did succeed in implementing some sort of discipline or taking some sort of disciplinary action. But Mr. Prosecutor, if you would have enough patience, I could tell you, for example, one way in which -- one -- something that happened in Travnik, after the fall of Jajce, what it actually looked like in practice. Would you allow me to do that? May I do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it about military discipline, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The way in which this was introduced or in which we tried to introduce this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, of course, sir, within a reasonable time limit, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place is Travnik. The year is 1992. The time is after the fall of Jajce. From one position, a group of soldiers, about 30 to 35 of them, fled, they left their positions, and I stopped them. I told them to go back. They said they didn't want to. I then asked that the commanders come forward and go to prison. Sir, when I say this, let me tell you that I did not have a prison, I did not have any military police, there was no law according to which I could try them. When they agreed to go to prison, then the rest of the people said, "Well, we are going to prison too." The prison that didn't exist, by the way. And I remembered to say on that occasion, "You can go to prison, but the uniform is not your own." And on threat, and by threats, by shouting and screaming at them, I demanded that they take off their uniforms and go to prison naked. As it was very cold, they reconsidered. And then we started talking and discussing the matter and I -- we invoked morals and ethics and the duty to defend the country from the Serbs who wanted to reach Sarajevo through the Lasva River valley. And three more figures, let me quote those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I told you I would give you a reasonable opportunity. Unless the Chamber wants to direct me otherwise, I think that's enough. Sir, don't you remember --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you remember HVO soldiers, for example, being imprisoned in certain parts of the Heliodrom for criminal violations or violations of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did try to introduce military discipline. That's true. And we did succeed from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall, just as one example, do you remember -- do you remember an HVO soldier by the name of Splico, who was held at the Heliodrom for using drugs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't remember that particular soldier, but I do know that the Heliodrom was a military investigation prison, investigative prison, under the competence of the military police of the Croatian Defence Council, and that we did try to take soldiers there who had violated discipline. We were more or less successful in this, depending. More successful if we were dealing with an individual but less successful if it was a group of individuals. All we could do was talk to the perpetrators and hold lectures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance again, please. Can the witness please be shown P415.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the man that you -- the gentleman that you had trouble remembering earlier, Zeljko Akrap, he was directly put under your command in May of 1993, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour. The witness -- it was not that the witness could not remember who Zeljko Akrap was during these proceedings. Quite the contrary. He answered straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, this man being placed on your immediate staff, under the command of Major General Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered you very precisely the first time, but let me repeat. When I arrived and took up my position as commander, I found Zeljko Akrap already there. I know him very well. He became a friend of mine from the war days. All I did not know was where he had come from exactly, that is to say, whether he had come from the Croatian army and what unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was the military district Split?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the collection -- one of the military districts in the organisation of the -- in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the base --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was an HV base of operations in Split, Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "base"? It was the headquarters of the Split district, in Split, of the HV, the Croatian army. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Mr. Akrap was being placed under your command, why was he being listed on the payroll of the military district in Split?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do not know that. You would have to ask Brigadier Miljenko Crnjac that. But what I can tell you is this. My answer is: The Croatian state endeavoured, either by giving money or in some other way, to compensate and remunerate people who went to war in Bosnia-Herzegovina on a voluntary basis. That is not contested. The people had to live on something. Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a state. We did not have any regular sources of income. We did not have a state or banks or the possibility of sending money. All we had was money collected on a voluntary basis and a very meager form of taxation, taxing the facilities that were still operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, why would the assistant to the minister, Miljenko Crnjac, in the HV army - and this stationery is under Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, Zagreb - why would an officer in Zagreb be putting an HV soldier under your command in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two answers to that question. First, in order to be very precise, in order to -- let me say that you ought to ask Minister Brigadier Crnjac himself. And my interpretation is as follows. A man would come and say that he wanted to go and fight down there, but he asked how he was going to do that and how -- that is to say how he would be ensured a minimum -- minimum money and financial resources to look after his family, and that was never contested. That is to say that the Croatian state helped, assisted, but did not send and did not order people to go. This is probably - and I repeat probably - just one of -- one way in which they endeavoured to ensure a minimum monthly income for that person's family during -- to keep them during the time he spent in the HVO as a volunteer in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In other words, sir, the Republic of Croatia actively assisted and supported the war against the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, I consider the thesis of this kind is a distortion of the facts, crude insinuations, and in short, insults.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could the witness please be shown --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Sir, based on your previous answers, perhaps we can anticipate your answer, but nonetheless I'll put it to you. This is an order that was -- or a request, excuse me. This is a request that was sent out over your name and rank and under your authorisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, something completely else. I did not ask for any private session before, but whenever a name was mentioned at the time when I was cross-examining, we went into private session. There are too many names mentioned here, and because of those people who might be called here as witnesses, and for some other reasons which I do not wish to mention in an open session, I would like to ask that we go into private session whenever names come up, because I really cannot say now, but you know that very many people here will be also coming as witnesses, and I do not wish their names to be interpreted by all sorts of media and to appear in the press with -- in a bad context. So may we go into private session whenever names come up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just say something? Mr. Krsnik said something that's very disturbing. You said that the newspapers in Bosnia and Herzegovina were reporting that General Praljak was being accused by this Tribunal or had been accused before the Tribunal. That's certainly how it translated to us, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke in the first private session this morning, then I said that General Praljak, during these seven years -- that you couldn't open a newspaper without that particular newspaper saying that he had been accused by the Prosecutor. Of course, he is here. He can testify to that also. And today, when I mentioned the press, I don't know what the interpretation was, but what I said was -- but we are already back in the open session. Today what I said was that the media, especially the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, will more or less, depending, of course, on the lobby and on the interest group, but of course mostly to make the work of the Defence more difficult. What I'm saying will be that General Praljak accused somebody here. You see, there was an article in the Bosnia-Herzegovina media about my opening address, and I can -- I am having it translated to show as an example of how this case is covered, that names of witnesses are disclosed, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, I understood you to say - and maybe I understood you incorrectly or the translation was incorrect - that the newspapers had said that General Praljak was accused. This is open session, and I do this deliberately. If this is being reported on the open waves, General Praljak has not been accused by this Tribunal and he is not being accused by this Tribunal. General Praljak is here as a witness and he is being treated with the courtesy that witnesses deserve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know where we left off, if the usher has provided the witness with Exhibit 559.3 or not. If so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you saw this document in direct examination. Does Mr. -- this officer that you've just told us a few things about, Mr. Matic, in fact confirm accommodations being made for a large number of soldiers coming from Croatia at the Heliodrom, outside of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key word here is "volunteer units," and during the examination-in-chief, I said that the overall number of soldiers, volunteers from Croatia, at its peak, did not exceed 800. And I stand by this statement, even though this figure, 800, holds true only for a short while at a time when we sought help because we were in a very difficult situation, and when we requested help not from the Croatian army but from people that we knew and people who came from the territory, who drew roots from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So where do you get the number 800? You seem to have a very specific number in mind. What's the source of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know exactly, but the source of this fact is the fact that 20 came from here and -- you know, Mr. Prosecutor, when I came in April 1992, I had seven soldiers from Sunja, from Croatia, with me who had -- they had volunteered. And I all deployed them with -- I put them up with Muslims so as to expedite their preparedness for what we knew was looming on the horizon, and that was the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the source of the number 800. That was my question. Sir, if you look at 559.3. Let me suggest to you, sir, that if you look at 559.3, if your number of 800 is anywhere close to being correct, the number on this one particular document alone represents over 400 people. That would be half the total number that you say were in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the war, would it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the key word is "announced," and believe me, less than a half of those truly arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher please give you Exhibit 592.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir -- well, again, does this appear to be an order, over your name, signed for, in fact, by your aid, Zeljko Akrap?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somebody did sign my name. Whether it is Zeljko Akrap's signature, after all this time, I wouldn't really be able to say. But somebody did sign it in my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that around this time, the 7th of September, 1993, Colonel Ivica Primorac was being sent to the Command-Staff School of the Republic of Croatia army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible. It's quite possible. Yes. The date could be correct. The date -- I tend to agree with the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The letter says: "Colonel Ivica Primorac, who is going to the Command-Staff School of the Croatian army, will be replaced on the position of assistant to the commander of the HVO Main Staff for the professional army by Colonel Dragan (Stipo) Curcic." Why was it necessary to give the notice of that replacement, as immediately up above, to the office of the chief of the HV Main Staff in Zagreb? Why would you have to notify somebody in Zagreb about a personnel move in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. Not about personnel changes but that Ivica Primorac would be going to the staff school in Croatia so as to raise the level of training and discipline of our army to a high level. During the war I also attended some of the manoeuvres of NATO in Germany, and somebody informed somebody that I would be coming, because that is how it is done. This is good manners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The purpose of this letter, sir, I'm going to suggest to you - you can certainly read it in the Croatian language - the purpose of this letter is not so much to inform about Mr. Primorac and what he's doing, but the point is: "Will be replaced on the position by Colonel Dragan Curcic." Now, why would you have to tell HVO Main Staff in Zagreb about who was replacing Mr. Primorac while he was away?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you showed such a letter to any professional soldier in the West, then you would see that it had been written by a layman, by a civilian, who was a civilian beforehand, because Mr. Zeljko Akrap was not a military, and that there is absolutely nothing that can be in dispute except that information in excess is provided, and that was not necessary. Mr. Dragan Curcic subsequently became the second-ranking man in the Federation. And I also need to mention that at no time during the negotiations - and that includes Dayton - the HVO was not a paramilitary force. It was recognised as a regular force of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is its status to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 661.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall proposing that a man named Ante Saskor - forgive my pronunciation - which is described here, in personal rank, colonel in the HV, do you remember proposing this man to be placed -- made the commander of the Mario Hrkac Cikota Brigade in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Ante Saskor from a place called Omis, near Split, where my mother was born. I asked him, I pleaded with him, because he's an outstanding -- a man of outstanding qualities, an honest man and a good soldier, so I pleaded with him to come and stay with the HVO as the commander in Siroki Brijeg, because before that, that brigade had fallen apart several times before that, for different reasons. And the qualities of that man, his human qualities to begin with - not his military qualities because he was not a soldier before the war - and owing to his human qualities, this brigade became a high-quality and good unit, and unfortunately he was subsequently killed in the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you say he was not a soldier before the war, but at this time as of October, 1993, he was a colonel in the Republic of Croatia army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he worked at the -- at the power plant in Omis as an electrician, and I presume that at that time, before I asked him to come as a volunteer, that he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the fall of 1992, you were the senior Croat officer commanding in connection with an armed conflict around Prozor with the Muslims, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a volunteer at the time. I was in Rama, Prozor, but not as a high-ranking officer of the Croatian Army but as Slobodan Praljak, volunteer. This high-ranking officer of the Croatian Army would mean that somebody had sent me on the basis of an official act, and that is not true. That is not true. And I was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were the senior commanding officer over the Bosnian Croat armed forces in Prozor -- in and around Prozor, in October, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I commanded those forces when we tried to liberate parts, and lines that had been dug behind our backs, above the town itself, 20 kilometres away from the front lines that we were holding against Serb and Montenegrin forces on the hills above Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on Tuesday in your testimony, you complained about the Muslims not assisting the Croats in defending Jajce against the Serbs in the autumn of 1992, and again approximately October, 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not complain, because I was not in Jajce. What I said was that one of the reasons for the relatively quick fall of Jajce was very poor combat between Jajce and Travnik and especially on Komar, which is a hill, because the route of supplies towards Jajce from the hill of Komar, which was held by the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was very narrow, and so the defence of Jajce was weakened and they were practically encircled, and that is how it fell into Chetniks' hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did the fall of Jajce -- did that happen before or after the Croat troops under your command in Prozor burned down most of the Muslim houses in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict in Prozor happened when I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I repeat my question to you: Was the fall of Jajce before or after Croat troops under your command - you told us a few moments ago you were in command - burned down most of the Muslim homes in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object, not to the question but the series of questions asked by the Prosecutor, and at the same time, the Prosecutor is attempting to testify and he therefore puts forth certain things which the witness never said. So I believe the question should either be reworded or he should be ordered by you to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think your question involved several questions. First of all, you have to establish whether there is burning down of the Muslim houses in Prozor, and then later on, you will ask about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember, for example - to get some more specifics - do you remember being in a meeting in Prozor with a Mr. Karic representing the Muslim side, around this time, in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in the area from Zagreb, and at the personal order - no, I misspoke - request of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Franjo Tudjman, to help quell the incident that took place in Prozor, I undertook to calm the situation with many Muslim commanders, Palic, Karic and others, and I endeavoured to carry out the job as properly as possible. That is correct. And we did succeed in calming the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, that when you were there, even after you arrived in, personally, in Prozor, that the Muslims houses were being burned and were on fire even at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In Prozor, I was in Prozor for a very short period of time, and then I continued the negotiations and talks in Jablanica, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall while were you in Prozor -- and I submit -- I put to you while Muslim houses were burning, that you joined HVO soldiers in a celebration in the middle of town. I think there was lamb on the spit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say to you, sir, two things. First, that that lamb on the spit was being rotated by some HOS units, that with a rifle I followed somebody, an asshole, who was following -- was running after a Muslim, and I say that you are lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's language that we really shouldn't hear in court. I'm sure it just slipped out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. I might have used a term that was stronger than the speaker was using.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that I did my job very honourably, that it is very difficult for me, that when I was trying to introduce order, I could have -- and I could have lost my head, to hear criticisms of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. She might have used an expression that was stronger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Not at all, Madam Interpreter. I'm used to strong language and we are dealing with war crimes. The word that I was objecting to was "lying," and I think it's better that neither witnesses nor counsel accuse people of lying. There are other words that you can use. That's the word I was objecting to, not anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will not happen again, although it is very painful to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think you confirmed both yesterday and today, if I heard you correctly, that Mr. Zeljko Siljeg was one of your subordinates at times when you were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe you also testified yesterday that another person who was subordinate to you at times when you were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina was this man Jure Schmidt. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While Mr. Siljeg was directly subordinate to me, Mr. Jurgen Schmidt was not directly to me, but indirectly subordinate, so that there was somebody in between him and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was between Mr. Schmidt and you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow that I cannot be specific and exact, I think it was Mr. Glasnovic, Mr. Zeljko Glasnovic, but I do put in a question mark when I say that. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, when you say "Zeljko," did you mean --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Glasnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 186.1? Mr. Usher, if you could perhaps move that up a bit on the page -- excuse me, on the ELMO, so that we could see a bit more of the text? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report -- appears to be a report from Mr. Schmidt to Colonel Zeljko Siljeg in person at 1810 hours on the 24th of October, 1992. And Mr. Schmidt reports at that time, first paragraph, "Constant combat activity. The town of Prozor and Rama Lake are under the control of the Prozor HV/HVO. These two areas are ethnically pure. The Muslim population has been detained or has fled." That's an accurate statement of what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was not at that place at that time. I said a moment ago I was requested by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and I went down there after that and did what I did, and I stand by that, and I'm very proud of having done what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you -- as a senior officer, you received reports, both in writing and orally, from your subordinates, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, sir, I was not at that time at that place, and as I was not there, I did not receive any reports at all. I arrived later on. I arrived in Gornji Vakuf, and as to the operation, that I knew what it was and why it took place and it was one and a half months after attempts to negotiate with the participation of all the international forces who were down there, I received reports, and I can tell you about that. As to what you have just said, it has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, was it not reported up the HVO chain of command that as the town of Prozor, as of the 24th of October, 1992, was ethnically pure, the Muslims had either been detained or had fled? That was reported up your chain of command, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, sir, I was not there. I was not performing any function and I was not part of the command chain. I think I am speaking clearly enough and in proper fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court will excuse me for just one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm hesitating because I look at the clock and where I am in the outline -- I was consulting with the case manager in terms of some material. While I hate to lose any time, of course, I suspect that if I start a new topic, there is no way we will finish it in the next five minutes. But I'll start if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have been advised that we have to be out of this room at quarter to 2.00 because this room will be used by another trial. So what if we stop here and we resume on Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'm sorry to say that we have to keep you here for the weekend, and as I said before to you, do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Have a nice weekend in The Hague. We will rise until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 25
